title: Time complexity of Gaussian agnostic halfspace learning
formal: Determine the optimal joint running-time dependence on dimension \(n\) and inverse excess error \(t=1/\varepsilon\) for agnostically learning affine halfspaces from Gaussian examples. Retain the source’s deterministic Boolean target-function model: for every measurable \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\{-1,+1\}\), a learner sees independent \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\), and must output a predictor \(h\) such that \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{err}_f(h)\le\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)+\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad \operatorname{err}_f(h)=\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)],\] where \[\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)=\inf_{w\in\mathbb R^n,\ b\in\mathbb R}\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[\operatorname{sgn}(\langle w,x\rangle+b)\ne f(x)].\] The parameters range over \(n\ge2\), \(t\ge3\). More precisely, characterize the asymptotically attainable uniform time bounds \(T(n,t)\) defined below, with matching algorithmic upper and general lower bounds in each stated parameter regime. The source’s subsidiary question about \(n^{O(\log t)}\) is recorded in context; it does not replace the broader optimal-time target. The real-arithmetic convention and its distinction from a finite-bit implementation are explicit parts of this formulation.
why: Gaussian inputs remove many distributional complications, yet arbitrary labels can still make even the best linear predictor difficult to match. The question asks for the precise computational cost of decreasing excess error, allowing any output representation. It separates the number of examples needed for learning from the much larger time used by current algorithms.
status_note: The broad optimal-time question remains without a checked matching resolution under the exact formulation given here. The 2014 Definition 4 uses a fixed target function and leaves real-input precision implicit; affine halfspaces are stated in its introduction. The completed record explicitly selects an exact-real arithmetic convention and preserves deterministic Boolean labels. COLT 2021 gives SQ optimality in a larger joint-label model. ICML 2023 gives conditional LWE hardness with stochastic labels, a sqrt(log n) exponent loss and a stated error range; a deterministic-label and exact-real lower-bound transfer was not established in this review. The 2026 proper and homogeneous results have their own output/runtime qualifications. These known theorems are substantive related progress, not a claimed constant-factor classification or unconditional resolution. Current status is uncertain after checks through 16 September 2026.

importance.reason: A central quantitative problem in computational learning theory. Strong modern SQ and cryptographic results clarify the error-dependent exponent, but exact optimization, label conventions, model of computation and uniform parameter regimes remain essential to interpreting the original question.

sentences: The card asks for optimal dimension and accuracy dependence when matching the best affine halfspace under Gaussian inputs.
It preserves the original deterministic Boolean target-function model and permits any finite evaluable predictor.
The statement explicitly counts exact real-arithmetic sampling, computation, output and evaluation and distinguishes this from finite-bit complexity.
Modern statistical-query, cryptographic and proper-learning results have different assumptions or interfaces whose transfer is not silently presumed.
A Lean resolution must characterize the attainable uniform time rates with matching bounds under the same label, resource and parameter conventions.

definitions:
\(\gamma_n\) is the Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R^n\) with density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\) with respect to Lebesgue measure; its coordinates are independent standard normal random variables. A halfspace predictor has the form \(x\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(\sum_i w_i x_i+b)\), with real coefficients and threshold and \(\operatorname{sgn}(z)=+1\) for \(z\ge0\), otherwise \(-1\). Constant predictors are allowed by \(w=0\). Affine halfspaces follow the source’s introductory definition, which includes a constant term; its later notation sometimes suppresses that term. No margin, bounded coefficient encoding, sparsity or homogeneity assumption is added. The infimum in \(\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)\) does not presume an available optimum or supply its value to the learner.

The unknown target \(f\) is any Borel-measurable Boolean function, fixed before the examples and learner coins are drawn. It need not itself be a halfspace. Each oracle request returns an independent Gaussian vector with its exact value under the same \(f\); the learner cannot choose the sampled point, inspect code for \(f\), ask for a label at a selected point, or query the optimum. There is no independent stochastic label distribution conditional on \(x\) in this literal target-function formulation. The outer success probability includes all sample draws and internal randomness; error is measured on a fresh Gaussian input. The learner may output an improper predictor. The source uses \(L^1\) notation: for \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued \(h,f\), \(\mathbb E|h-f|=2\operatorname{err}_f(h)\). Thus excess disagreement \(1/t\) is excess \(L^1\) loss \(2/t\), not \(1/t\). This exact factor is kept separate from asymptotic runtime notation.

Computational convention: use one finite uniform real-arithmetic register program, with rational constants in its fixed code, integer control and rational public parameters \(n,t\). It can copy real registers, apply \(+,-,\times,\div\) to a constant number of registers, compare their values, branch and generate a fair random bit, each at unit arithmetic cost. Division by zero must be handled by a comparison before division. Discrete control, register access and writing an output instruction each cost one step. Sampling and loading an \(n\)-coordinate labeled example costs \(n+1\) units. The oracle supplies exact real coordinates; no cost for internally generating a Gaussian real is attributed to the learner. There is no floor, digit-extraction primitive, arbitrary real advice, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or decision oracle for general properties of real numbers. Uniformity means the same finite program works for all \(n,t,f\), with no length-dependent constants or advice.

The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit on \(n\) real inputs, built from the same operations, Boolean choices and sign tests. Constants may be stored real values computed during training. It must define a total \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued predictor on every real input, with each division guarded when its denominator vanishes. Output writing and each stored real coefficient are charged one unit per written item. Evaluation cost is the number of circuit operations; it is included in the resource measure. Such circuits give measurable predictors and need no further examples or target access after training. There is no requirement that the output be a halfspace, and no fixed polynomial degree or circuit-size restriction beyond the stated time bound.

For a learner \(A\), let \(\tau_A(n,t)\) be the supremum over every allowed target, sample history and coin history of its training cost plus the evaluation cost of its output circuit, with nontermination or invalid output charged infinite cost. A computable nondecreasing positive integer function \(T(n,t)\) is an attainable asymptotic time bound if there are one such uniform learner \(A\) and a constant \(K\ge1\), independent of \(n,t,f\), such that the PAC guarantee holds for every \(n,t,f\) and \(\tau_A(n,t)\le K T(n,t)\) for every \(n\ge2,t\ge3\). Characterizing optimal complexity means an explicit description of which rates are attainable, up to constant factors, rather than a pointwise infimum over a different hard-coded algorithm for each parameter pair. The dependence on both parameters must remain visible; any restriction such as \(t\le n^c\) must be stated for that bound. No single asymptotically fastest uniform algorithm is assumed to exist in advance.

This exact-real arithmetic model is an explicitly stated convention completing the source’s continuous-example interface. It does not assert a theorem translating arbitrary real computations to the bit model. Exact Gaussian examples have no finite binary representation in general, and the 2014 question specifies neither a rounding oracle nor a coordinate-bit budget. A separate bit-complexity variant would need those definitions and a proof that rounding preserves the learning guarantee for arbitrary measurable targets. Numerical rounding is therefore not silently included as a free primitive in the present arithmetic target.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean-checked asymptotic classification of the attainable bounds just defined: explicit noncircular conditions on \(T(n,t)\), together with proofs of attainability for the asserted upper rates and impossibility for the excluded lower rates. An optimal-rate expression must have matching bounds with the same dimension/error regimes and cost convention. If a fastest uniform rate is not attained, describe and prove the resulting attainable-rate structure instead of assuming a pointwise optimum corresponds to one algorithm. An upper bound alone, a conditional obstruction alone, or a matching result only for statistical-query algorithms does not determine the unrestricted optimum. Computational assumptions must remain hypotheses of the relevant partial result. A lower bound with stochastic labels or a restricted proper output must establish its applicability to the deterministic-target, improper-output interface before being used here. A proof about finite-bit computation must likewise establish a relation to the specified real-arithmetic model. The requested precision is matching asymptotic rates up to constants, not an additive approximation to a numerical value.

source_formulation.text: What is the optimal time complexity of Gaussian agnostic halfspace learning; in particular, can the dimension exponent be only logarithmic in inverse excess error?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: A halfspace classifies points by which side of a hyperplane they occupy. In an agnostic task, the labels need not be linearly separable: the benchmark is the least disagreement achievable by a halfspace, plus a requested excess error. A regular Gaussian input marginal does not itself constrain the complexity of the labeling rule.

The 2014 paper contrasts the known \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}\) algorithmic scale with a sparse-noisy-parity-based conditional \(n^{\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))}\) obstruction. Its Question 3 asks for the optimal time and explicitly proposes \(n^{O(\log(1/\varepsilon))}\) as a possibility. The quoted lower scale comes from a reduction and a hardness premise; it is not an unconditional time lower bound.

Definition 4 of the source labels examples by a deterministic target function and states an L¹ approximation guarantee; its halfspace discussion also uses Boolean classification language. Later papers often start directly from an arbitrary joint distribution on features and labels. An upper guarantee for all such joint distributions includes deterministic labels as a special case. A lower bound for the larger family does not automatically apply to the deterministic subfamily.

COLT 2021 Diakonikolas–Kane–Pittas–Zarifis proves essentially matching \(n^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon^2)}\)-scale statistical-query hardness for halfspaces in its general joint-distribution model. Statistical queries return approximate expectations of bounded test functions instead of the actual independent examples. This is an important optimality theorem for that restricted access model, not a lower bound for every sample-based learner in the present formulation.

ICML 2023 Diakonikolas–Kane–Ren gives a stronger related cryptographic obstruction. Its Corollary 3.2, under Assumption 2.3 on subexponential LWE hardness, excludes time \(n^{O((1/(\varepsilon\sqrt{\log n}))^\alpha)}\) for every fixed \(0<\alpha<2\), in its stated range \(c/(\sqrt n\log n)\le\varepsilon\le1/(\log n)^\gamma\), with \(\gamma>1/2\) and the specified sufficiently large constant \(c\). Both the logarithmic loss in the exponent and the error range are material. The theorem uses arbitrary joint labels and a computational cryptographic reduction; it is not an unconditional constant-factor characterization of this real-arithmetic deterministic-label problem.

The 2023 hard-instance construction contains residual random noise in the labels even after conditioning on the Gaussian feature vector, and its null case has independent fair labels. This review has not established a conversion of that construction into a fixed deterministic target with the same computational costs. Nor does a finite-bit cryptographic assumption by itself give a lower bound against unit-cost exact-real programs. Those interface gaps are stated explicitly rather than hidden by a claim that the original question is fully resolved.

Tikhonov–Vasilyan’s May 2026 Theorem 3.14 outputs an affine halfspace with error \(\operatorname{OPT}+\varepsilon\) and time \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}+(1/\varepsilon)^{O(1/\varepsilon^{2.5})}\) at constant confidence. Its general joint-label guarantee includes fixed deterministic targets, and proper output is allowed by an improper-learning task. The theorem advances proper learning and matches the known dimension exponent; its additional accuracy-only term and continuous computational conventions must remain visible in a joint optimal-time comparison. No finite-bit equivalence is claimed here.

The April 2026 Huang–Juba paper studies a further related problem with homogeneous halfspace output and general joint labels. Its LWE-based hardness is stated with those restrictions. Homogeneous proper learning is not substituted for unrestricted improper affine learning, and the computational assumption is not asserted true.

The original source does not fix coordinate precision or a universal elementary cost model for real samples. This card states a real-arithmetic convention so the resource question can be read precisely. Its current-status review remains uncertain: the inspected recent results explain substantial progress but do not certify a matching resolution with all the displayed label, computation and parameter conventions.
